Reading The Operator Surface¶

Duration-duration arithmetic combines elapsed values elementwise and applies ordinary N-D broadcasting. Unary minus reverses direction. Integer multiplication and division scale elapsed nanoseconds; there is no implicit floating scalar overload and no plain-number addition, because those call forms would leave the unit ambiguous.

+= and -= are the only mutating operators. They replace the receiver and return Duration&; all other arithmetic operators allocate a result. Signed nanosecond overflow throws rather than wrapping. Division by zero also throws. NaT propagates through arithmetic.

Every comparison is elementwise and returns a shape-preserving Boolean Series, not one host bool. This permits broadcasting and masking. NaT does not compare as an elapsed value: use isnat() when absence itself is the question.

Stream insertion uses the same renderer as pluss::duration::print(). It preserves shape and prints negative spans with normalized day and clock fields.

Examples¶

Example 1. Binary, unary, and scalar arithmetic.

auto hour = pluss::duration::hours(1);
auto ninety = pluss::duration::minutes(90);

std::cout << (hour + ninety) << "\n";
std::cout << -hour << "\n";
std::cout << hour * 3 << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::duration::days(1) / 4;

These produce 2:30, -1:00, 3:00, and 6:00 elapsed durations, respectively. Division truncates at integral nanosecond precision.

Example 2. Compound assignment mutates and remains equivalent to its binary counterpart.

auto value = hour;
value += ninety;
std::cout << pluss::series::print(value.eq(hour + ninety));

value -= ninety;
std::cout << pluss::series::print(value.eq(hour));

Both checks print scalar true Boolean Series. Broadcasting rules are the same as for + and -; mutation does not weaken shape validation.

Example 3. Comparisons build masks rather than collapsing an array.

auto left = pluss::duration::minutes({30, 60, 90});
auto right = pluss::duration::hours(1);
std::cout << pluss::series::print(left < right) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::series::print(left >= right);

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[true, false, false]
Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[false, true, true]

Example 4. Direct streaming and the named printer are identical.

auto value = pluss::duration::minutes(90);
std::ostringstream out;
out << value;
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << (out.str() == pluss::duration::print(value));

Output¶

true

Example 5. Negative sub-day output is floor-normalized.

std::cout << pluss::duration::nanos(-1);

Output¶

Duration(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1)
-1 days 23:59:59.999999999

Example 6. Overflow is a checked failure.

auto high = pluss::duration::nanos(
    (std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::max)());
auto one = pluss::duration::nanos(1);
try {
  (void)(high + one);
} catch (const pluss::Error& error) {
  const std::string message = error.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

Duration::operator+: nanosecond overflow

Neighboring Named Methods¶

The dedicated add, sub, neg, mul, and div pages teach each arithmetic contract in isolation. eq through ge do the same for comparisons. floordiv() and mod() are named methods because C++ has no distinct operator for floor division and the public remainder takes a nanosecond integer.
